questions: What is the exact definition of "sum of B^p" - does this mean we compute B^p for each possible matrix B and then add all resulting matrices element-wise?
How is matrix exponentiation B^p defined when B contains elements that might be zero after replacement, and what happens if p exceeds the matrix dimension N?
When computing the sum over all possible matrices B, are we summing the individual matrix elements or the entire matrices as mathematical objects?
What is the expected time complexity constraint for this problem given the potentially exponential number of matrices (p-1)^K?
How should the case be handled when p = 1, making the range [1, p-1] empty since p-1 = 0?
Is the matrix multiplication for computing B^p performed in the field of integers modulo p, and should intermediate calculations also be done modulo p?
What constitutes the "number of zeros K" - is this counting all zero elements in the original matrix A before any replacements?
Should the final output matrix elements be reduced modulo p even if they are already in the range [0, p-1] due to the summation process?
answers: Yes. For each possible matrix B obtained by replacing zeros with values 1 to p-1, compute B^p, then sum all resulting matrices element-wise.
Matrix exponentiation B^p is standard repeated matrix multiplication. p can exceed N; only standard matrix multiplication is used.
We sum entire matrices element-wise: for each position, sum the corresponding elements from all possible B^p matrices.
The problem expects efficient computation within the given constraints; analyze the pattern rather than enumerate all matrices.
When p = 1, there is only one valid value (1) for each zero replacement since p must be prime and p ≥ 2 per constraints.
Yes. All calculations, including matrix multiplication and exponentiation, must be performed modulo p.
K is the total count of zero elements in the original matrix A.
Yes. All final output elements must be reduced modulo p.
